messages.subject: what laptop to buy ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am about to buy a new laptop and was wondering which one to get. I am prepared to pay about 3000 USD.

I want it to be performant for stuff we talk about on this list (i.e., JAGS, NIMBLE, sims in R, ...) and so I thought I want a fast processor and 64 GB RAM. My current favourite is a DELL XPS, of which I can get a 16' machine with 1 TB HD, 64 GB RAM and some late i9 processor for that price. Alternative might be an HP Z book.

Any thoughts or advice ? (Note: I do NOT want a gamer machine.)

Thanks and best regards  ----  Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hello Marc,

I went with the ThinkPad P1 Gen 5 (16″ Intel) mobile workstation last year (32 GB RAM, i7 processor, and 1 TB SSD) and have really enjoyed it. I, too, did not want a gaming laptop and had a bad experience with a Dell laptop prior to purchasing the ThinkPad. That being said, I've had good luck with Dell machines, but prefer ThinkPads.

I see that it is no longer available, but the ThinkPad P14s Gen 5 Intel (14″) Mobile Workstation (~$2500) looks really nice and it can be customized to include a 2 TB SSD hard drive and 96 GB of RAM. One advantage to this laptop (which is my only complaint about my current laptop), is that the "Ctrl" and "fn" buttons are in the standard place on the keyboard.

Good luck!

Alexej

Hello all,

I am working on a Barker model to estimate survival and have gotten stuck trying to figure out goodness-of-fit testing. I have encounter data from a primary site and encounter data from outside the primary site over an 11-year period. I’ve fixed the recovery parameter in the model at zero since dead recoveries are very uncommon for the species and I have none in my dataset. I’ve based my model on the example in Riecke et al. (2021) <https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ecs2.3810> and examples from Kéry and Schaub (2012). Here is the JAGS code for a simplified version of the model:

model {

# -------------------------------------------------
# Parameters:
# s: survival probability
# F: fidelity probability
# p: inside resighting probability
# R: outside resighting probability given survival from t to t+1
# Rp: outside resighting probability given mortality during interval t to t+1
# f: recovery probability
# -------------------------------------------------
# States (S):
# 1 alive in study area
# 2 alive outside study area
# 3 recently dead and recovered
# 4 recently dead, resighted
# 5 dead in previous interval
# Observations (O):
# 1 seen in, seen out
# 2 seen in, not seen out
# 3 not seen in, seen out
# 4 not seen in, not seen out
# 5 recovered
# -------------------------------------------------

# Priors and constraints
for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
   s[t] <- mean.s
   F[t] <- mean.F
   p[t] <- mean.p
   R[t] <- mean.R
   Rp[t] <- mean.Rp
   f[t] <- mean.f
   }
mean.s ~ dbeta(1, 1)     # Prior for mean survival
mean.F ~ dbeta(1, 1)     # Prior for mean fidelity
mean.p ~ dbeta(1, 1)     # Prior for mean resighting
mean.R ~ dbeta(1, 1)     # Prior for mean resighting outside given survival
mean.Rp ~ dbeta(1, 1)    # Prior for mean resighting outside given mortality
mean.f <- 0     # Prior for mean recovery

# Define state-transition and observation matrices
for (i in 1:nind){
   # Define probabilities of state S(t+1) given S(t)
   for (t in first[i]:(n.occasions-1)){
      ps[1,i,t,1] <- s[t]*F[t]
      ps[1,i,t,2] <- s[t]*(1-F[t])
      ps[1,i,t,3] <- (1-s[t])*f[t]
      ps[1,i,t,4] <- (1-s[t])*Rp[t]*(1-f[t])
      ps[1,i,t,5] <- (1-s[t])*(1-Rp[t])*(1-f[t])
      ps[2,i,t,1] <- 0
      ps[2,i,t,2] <- s[t]
      ps[2,i,t,3] <- (1-s[t])*f[t]
      ps[2,i,t,4] <- (1-s[t])*Rp[t]*(1-f[t])
      ps[2,i,t,5] <- (1-s[t])*(1-Rp[t])*(1-f[t])
      ps[3,i,t,1] <- 0
      ps[3,i,t,2] <- 0
      ps[3,i,t,3] <- 0
      ps[3,i,t,4] <- 0
      ps[3,i,t,5] <- 1
      ps[4,i,t,1] <- 0
      ps[4,i,t,2] <- 0
      ps[4,i,t,3] <- 0
      ps[4,i,t,4] <- 0
      ps[4,i,t,5] <- 1
      ps[5,i,t,1] <- 0
      ps[5,i,t,2] <- 0
      ps[5,i,t,3] <- 0
      ps[5,i,t,4] <- 0
      ps[5,i,t,5] <- 1

      # Define probabilities of O(t) given S(t)
      po[1,i,t,1] <- p[t]*R[t]
      po[1,i,t,2] <- p[t]*(1-R[t])
      po[1,i,t,3] <- (1-p[t])*R[t]
      po[1,i,t,4] <- (1-p[t])*(1-R[t])
      po[1,i,t,5] <- 0
      po[2,i,t,1] <- 0
      po[2,i,t,2] <- 0
      po[2,i,t,3] <- R[t]
      po[2,i,t,4] <- 1-R[t]
      po[2,i,t,5] <- 0
      po[3,i,t,1] <- 0
      po[3,i,t,2] <- 0
      po[3,i,t,3] <- 0
      po[3,i,t,4] <- 0
      po[3,i,t,5] <- 1
      po[4,i,t,1] <- 0
      po[4,i,t,2] <- 0
      po[4,i,t,3] <- 1
      po[4,i,t,4] <- 0
      po[4,i,t,5] <- 0
      po[5,i,t,1] <- 0
      po[5,i,t,2] <- 0
      po[5,i,t,3] <- 0
      po[5,i,t,4] <- 1
      po[5,i,t,5] <- 0
      } #t
   } #i

# Likelihood
for (i in 1:nind){
   # Define latent state at first capture
   z[i,first[i]] <- y[i,first[i]]
   for (t in (first[i]+1):n.occasions){
      # State process: draw S(t) given S(t-1)
      z[i,t] ~ dcat(ps[z[i,t-1], i, t-1,])
      # Observation process: draw O(t) given S(t)
      y[i,t] ~ dcat(po[z[i,t], i, t-1,])
      } #t

model {

# -------------------------------------------------
# Parameters:
# s: survival probability
# F: fidelity probability
# p: inside resighting probability
# R: outside resighting probability given survival from t to t+1
# Rp: outside resighting probability given mortality during interval t to t+1
# f: recovery probability
# -------------------------------------------------
# States (S):
# 1 alive in study area
# 2 alive outside study area
# 3 recently dead and recovered
# 4 recently dead, resighted
# 5 dead in previous interval
# Observations (O):
# 1 seen in, seen out
# 2 seen in, not seen out
# 3 not seen in, seen out
# 4 not seen in, not seen out
# 5 recovered
# -------------------------------------------------

# Priors and constraints
for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
   s[t] <- mean.s
   F[t] <- mean.F
   p[t] <- mean.p
   R[t] <- mean.R
   Rp[t] <- mean.Rp
   f[t] <- mean.f
   }
mean.s ~ dbeta(1, 1)     # Prior for mean survival
mean.F ~ dbeta(1, 1)     # Prior for mean fidelity
mean.p ~ dbeta(1, 1)     # Prior for mean resighting
mean.R ~ dbeta(1, 1)     # Prior for mean resighting outside given survival
mean.Rp ~ dbeta(1, 1)    # Prior for mean resighting outside given mortality
mean.f ~ dbeta(1, 1)     # Prior for mean recovery

# Define state-transition and reencounter probabilities - note no i index - is no longer individual
  for (t in 1:(n.occasions-1)){
      ps[1,t,1] <- s[t]*F[t]
      ps[1,t,2] <- s[t]*(1-F[t])
      ps[1,t,3] <- (1-s[t])*f[t]
      ps[1,t,4] <- (1-s[t])*Rp[t]*(1-f[t])
      ps[1,t,5] <- (1-s[t])*(1-Rp[t])*(1-f[t])
      ps[2,t,1] <- 0
      ps[2,t,2] <- s[t]
      ps[2,t,3] <- (1-s[t])*f[t]
      ps[2,t,4] <- (1-s[t])*Rp[t]*(1-f[t])
      ps[2,t,5] <- (1-s[t])*(1-Rp[t])*(1-f[t])
      ps[3,t,1] <- 0
      ps[3,t,2] <- 0
      ps[3,t,3] <- 0
      ps[3,t,4] <- 0
      ps[3,t,5] <- 1
      ps[4,t,1] <- 0
      ps[4,t,2] <- 0
      ps[4,t,3] <- 0
      ps[4,t,4] <- 0
      ps[4,t,5] <- 1
      ps[5,t,1] <- 0
      ps[5,t,2] <- 0
      ps[5,t,3] <- 0
      ps[5,t,4] <- 0
      ps[5,t,5] <- 1

      # Define probabilities of O(t) given S(t)
      po[1,t,1] <- p[t]*R[t]
      po[1,t,2] <- p[t]*(1-R[t])
      po[1,t,3] <- (1-p[t])*R[t]
      po[1,t,4] <- (1-p[t])*(1-R[t])
      po[1,t,5] <- 0
      po[2,t,1] <- 0
      po[2,t,2] <- 0
      po[2,t,3] <- R[t]
      po[2,t,4] <- 1-R[t]
      po[2,t,5] <- 0
      po[3,t,1] <- 0
      po[3,t,2] <- 0
      po[3,t,3] <- 0
      po[3,t,4] <- 0
      po[3,t,5] <- 1
      po[4,t,1] <- 0
      po[4,t,2] <- 0
      po[4,t,3] <- 1
      po[4,t,4] <- 0
      po[4,t,5] <- 0
      po[5,t,1] <- 0
      po[5,t,2] <- 0
      po[5,t,3] <- 0
      po[5,t,4] <- 1
      po[5,t,5] <- 0

    # Calculate probability of non-encounter (dq) and reshape the array for the encounter probabilities - below here says the same
    for (s in 1:ns){
      dp[s,t,s] <- po[s,t]
      dq[s,t,s] <- 1-po[s,t]
    } # s
    for (s in 1:(ns-1)){
      for (m in (s+1):ns){
        dp[s,t,m] <- 0
        dq[s,t,m] <- 0
      } # s
    } # m
    for (s in 2:ns){
      for (m in 1:(s-1)){
        dp[s,t,m] <- 0
        dq[s,t,m] <- 0
      } # s
    } # m
  } #t

  # Define the multinomial likelihood
  for (t in 1:((n.occasions-1)*ns)){
    marr[t,1:(n.occasions*ns-(ns-1))] ~ dmulti(pr[t,], rel[t])
  }

  # Define the cell probabilities of the multistate m-array
  # Define matrix U: product of probabilities of state-transition and non-encounter (this is just done because there is no product function for matrix multiplication in JAGS)
  for (t in 1:(n.occasions-2)){
    U[(t-1)*ns+(1:ns), (t-1)*ns+(1:ns)] <- ones
    for (j in (t+1):(n.occasions-1)){
      U[(t-1)*ns+(1:ns), (j-1)*ns+(1:ns)] <- U[(t-1)*ns+(1:ns), (j-2)*ns+(1:ns)] %*% ps[,t,] %*% dq[,t,]
    }
  }
  U[(n.occasions-2)*ns+(1:ns), (n.occasions-2)*ns+(1:ns)] <- ones
  # Diagonal
  for (t in 1:(n.occasions-2)){
    pr[(t-1)*ns+(1:ns),(t-1)*ns+(1:ns)] <- U[(t-1)*ns+(1:ns),(t-1)*ns+(1:ns)] %*% ps[,t,] %*% dp[,t,]
    # Above main diagonal
    for (j in (t+1):(n.occasions-1)){
      pr[(t-1)*ns+(1:ns), (j-1)*ns+(1:ns)] <- U[(t-1)*ns+(1:ns), (j-1)*ns+(1:ns)] %*% ps[,j,] %*% dp[,j,]
    }

  # Below main diagonal
  for (t in 2:(n.occasions-1)){
    for (j in 1:(t-1)){
      pr[(t-1)*ns+(1:ns),(j-1)*ns+(1:ns)] <- zero
    } #j
  } #t

  # Last column: probability of non-recapture
  for (t in 1:((n.occasions-1)*ns)){
    pr[t,(n.occasions*ns-(ns-1))] <- 1-sum(pr[t,1:((n.occasions-1)*ns)])
  } #t

  # Compute fit statistics for observed data
  for (t in 1:((n.occasions-1)*ns)){
    for (j in 1:(n.occasions*ns-(ns-1))){
      expmarr[t,j] <- rel[t]*pr[t,j]
      E.org[t,j] <- pow((pow(marr[t,j], 0.5)-pow(expmarr[t,j], 0.5)), 2)
    } #j
  } #t
  # Generate replicate data and compute fit stats from them
  for (t in 1:((n.occasions-1)*ns)){
    marr.new <http://marr.new>[t,1:(n.occasions*ns-(ns-1))] ~ dmulti(pr[t, ], rel[t])
    for (j in 1:(n.occasions*ns-(ns-1))){
      E.new[t,j] <- pow((pow(marr.new <http://marr.new>[t,j], 0.5)-pow(expmarr[t,j], 0.5)), 2)
    } #j
  } #t
  fit <- sum(E.org[,])
  fit.new <http://fit.new> <- sum(E.new[,])
}

I think my problem might be that the observation matrix is a matrix and not a vector (I have po[s,t,s] rather than po[s,t]), which doesn’t translate to the m-array format. I’m getting a JAGS error “Dimension mismatch taking subset of po”. Is there a way to convert this model to an m-array format? Or an alternate way to assess goodness-of-fit for the state-space formulation?

Thanks very much!
Amie

messages.body_plain:
Hello all!

I am sure many of you are familiar with testing our models by simulation (as nicely depicted e.g. in BPA, Kery & Schaub 2012). We choose true parameter values θ, then we generate N datasets and on each of those we run the model we want to test. Then we can calculate the bias by averaging the estimates from all the N models and subtract the true parameter value.

But, how to statistically test if the bias is significantly different from zero? To make the judgement if the model/estimator is biased or unbiased.

We could look at the percentage of confidence intervals containing the true parameter value θ
 (is this called the coverage of CI?). For biased estimator, we would expect this to be lower than 95% - but again, how much lower, how much difference would be significant to tell that this estimator is biased? But this method is not enough, the model could also just appear unbiased by giving wider confidence intervals than necessary, so precision should be also somehow tested?

I am unable to find any resource on this. E.g. DiRenzo et al. 2023 (10.1111/2041-210X.14030) doesn't resolve this.

Thank you very much!

PS: I posted the question also here: https://stats.stackexchange.com/q/655113/5509

Dear Tomas,

I don't know the "correct" approach (e.g., what statisticians say in their own journals). However, I'd not worry about a formal approach to this decision problem, but rather just eyeball this. If you run 100 simreps or ideally 1000 or more, and the mean of these is really close to the true value, then I'd consider the estimator as unbiased or nearly so. And I'd write something like "did not suggest any bias".

I also note that in spite of its value and intuitive appeal, we should not overestimate the importance of unbiasedness: for instance, we are happy to work with biased estimators whenever we use random effects or some (other) kind of penalization.

messages.body_plain:
Hello Tomas,

Yeah, I agree with Marc here. Perhaps a middle ground approach would be to calculate the mean and standard deviation of the relative absolute deviation (RAD) between the point estimates and the known parameters. This is a straightforward approach that was outlined in a recent paper (Berg et al. 2024 <http://10.1002/wlb3.01288>). That being said, I think you'll still make the same interpretations as you would taking the standard approach that Marc suggested.

Alexej

> I am sure many of you are familiar with testing our models by simulation (as nicely depicted e.g. in BPA, Kery & Schaub 2012). We choose true parameter values θ, then we generate N datasets and on each of those we run the model we want to test. Then we can calculate the bias by averaging the estimates from all the N models and subtract the true parameter value.
>
> But, how to statistically test if the bias is significantly different from zero? To make the judgement if the model/estimator is biased or unbiased.
>
> We could look at the percentage of confidence intervals containing the true parameter value θ
>  (is this called the coverage of CI?). For biased estimator, we would expect this to be lower than 95% - but again, how much lower, how much difference would be significant to tell that this estimator is biased? But this method is not enough, the model could also just appear unbiased by giving wider confidence intervals than necessary, so precision should be also somehow tested?
